paragraphs.source_en: It was indeed a hard letter to read. Not only was the penmanship poor, but it was altogether spelt in hiragana (cursive characters) with no punctuation marks. Where it began, or where it ended, was impossible to tell, and great pains were taken to punctuate it myself. A reward of five yen would hardly induce me to read such a long hard letter, as I am such a hasty, driving soul. But as it had come from Kiyo, I patiently went through it from beginning to end. Yes, I went through it, but as it took a great deal of pains in going over it, I remembered very little what was in it. So again, I began from the beginning. The room having got a little darker made it a little harder to read, and I at last went out to the edge of the veranda where, with my legs dangled down, I continued to read patiently, when a wind of early fall sprang up; shook the broad leaves of banana plants in the garden; gave its cool breath on my body, and on its return took on its wings the letter I had been intently reading out into the garden to the length of four or more feet with a rustling sound. Had I been poetical enough to let it go, the paper might have flown off to the hedge beyond. How could I be so imaginative at the moment? I was too busy reading the letter. Kiyo went on writing: "My dear Botchan, your character is as straight as an arrow, and I like it, but I am anxious about your quick temper with a word and a blow. Do not give people nicknames, for the act will draw enmity upon yourself. Do stop it, or only let me know by letter if you have had to do it at all. I have been told that the people in the country are bad, so do not be off guard lest you should be cruelly handled. It goes without saying that even the climate down there is worse than it is in Tokyo. Please wrap up your body well with bed clothing when you go to bed, or you will catch cold. Botchan's letter is too short to know
